sec.title: Background
sec.p: This single-center, open-label, exploratory trial aimed to investigate the efficacy and safety of envafolimab combined with lenvatinib and chemotherapy in previous treated advanced G/GEJ adenocarcinoma.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Eligible patients with HER2-negative, microsatellite stable (MSS) advanced G/GEJ adenocarcinoma who had progressed after first-line treatment were enrolled in this phase II trial. Patients without previously receiving PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors were enrolled in Group A, and those who progressed on the first-line PD-1 inhibitors were included in Group B. Patients in both groups received envafolimab (200 mg, subcutaneous injection (sc), days 1 and 15, Q4W) combined with lenvatinib and albumin-bound paclitaxel (100 mg/m2, IV, days 1, 8 and 15, Q4W, up to 6 cycles) until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, or refusal of continuation. The primary endpoint was objective response rate (ORR).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A total of 30 patients were included for safety and efficacy analysis. As of data cutoff (Sep 14, 2024), the median follow-up was 17.0 months (IQR: 8.0–18.8) in Group A. The ORR was 60.0%, and the DCR was 100.0%. The mPFS was 8.2 months (95% CI 6.1–10.4) with mOS of 14.8 months (95% CI 7.4–22.2). With a median follow-up of 9.0 months (IQR: 6.1–16.2) in Group B, the ORR was 46.7%, and the DCR was 100.0%. The mPFS was 5.9 months (95% CI 3.8–8.1), and the mOS was 11.5 months (95% CI 3.1–19.9). The overall incidence of adverse events (AEs) of any grade was 100%. While Group A showed numerically better outcomes than Group B, there was no statistically significant difference in PFS (P = 0.629) or OS (P = 0.873) between the two groups.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Second-line envafolimab-based combination therapy demonstrated promising effects in previously treated advanced GC, particularly in those who have not previously received ICIs.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Gastric cancer (GC) ranks as the fifth most prevalent malignant neoplasm globally and the fourth leading cause of cancer-related mortality [1]. The majority of patients are diagnosed at advanced stages, and systemic chemotherapy is the primary treatment modality for metastatic GC. Conventional chemotherapy yields a median overall survival (OS) of 12 months for advanced gastric cancer (AGC) patients, with cytotoxic agents such as fluoropyrimidine, platinum, taxanes, and irinotecan serving as the cornerstone of AGC therapy [2–4]. Specifically, the combination of fluoropyrimidine (fluorouracil, capecitabine, or S-1) with platinum is commonly utilized as the foundational regimen in initial treatment protocols [5–7].

The conventional second-line chemotherapy options, including paclitaxel, docetaxel, and irinotecan, exhibit comparable efficacy but varying toxicity profiles. [8–10] The ABSOLUTE trial demonstrated that weekly nab-paclitaxel administration achieved a superior ORR and lower toxicity compared to weekly solvent-based paclitaxel administration, with non-inferior OS, underscoring the enhanced potential benefits of nab-paclitaxel formulation as a second-line GC therapy [11, 12]. However, evidence from randomized trials indicates that combining multiple chemotherapeutic agents in second-line therapy does not improve survival outcomes compared to single-agent chemotherapy [8, 9].

The anti-vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR)-2 monoclonal antibody ramucirumab alone or in combination with paclitaxel prolongs the survival time, as proven in the REGARD and RAINBOW randomized phase III trials. Thus, paclitaxel used in combination with ramucirumab has become the standard second-line treatment for AGC [13, 14]. The efficacy of fruquintinib, a small-molecule inhibitor of VEGFR-1, VEGFR-2, and VEGFR-3, was proven in the FRUTIGA randomized phase III trial. [15, 16] Combination treatment with fruquintinib and paclitaxel is also expected to become a standard second-line regimen for AGC.

First-line chemotherapeutic drugs combined with the PD-1 antibody improves survival in patients with GC [7, 17, 18], while the effects of the combination with second-line chemotherapy and PD-1 antibody (with or without antiangiogenic agents) on outcomes remain unclear. After first-line PD-1 antibody treatment fails, it is still unknown whether switching to second-line programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) antibody or re-challenging with PD-1 antibody treatment is effective.

Envafolimab is a humanized camel-derived single-domain anti-PD-L1 antibody that is fused with a human immunoglobulin Fc fragment to prolong its half-life. Envafolimab, which is the first subcutaneous PD-L1-targeting single-domain antibody for treating cancers, represents a potentially convenient administration option for patients with MSI-H cancers [19, 20]. Given the established efficacy of ramucirumab plus paclitaxel as standard second-line therapy, we selected lenvatinib—a multi-kinase inhibitor targeting VEGFR-1, VEGFR-2, VEGFR-3, FGFR, PDGFR, and RET—based on its distinct mechanism of action and potential to modulate the tumor immune microenvironment by reducing tumor-associated macrophages and enhancing CD8 + T cell infiltration [24]. Preclinical and early clinical data (EPOC1706) supported the combination of lenvatinib with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors in gastric cancer [24]. Therefore, this exploratory phase II trial was performed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of a combination regimen (nab-paclitaxel, lenvatinib, and the anti-PD-L1 antibody envafolimab) in the second-line treatment of patients with Advanced G/GEJ adenocarcinoma.

sec.title: Study design and participants
sec.p: This prospective, open-label, single-center, exploratory phase II trial was conducted at Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center. Eligible patients between the ages of 18 and 80 years had histologically confirmed advanced metastatic gastric/gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma with a negative HER2 status. Eligible patients had experienced failure of previous first-line therapy. Two cohorts were included in our trial. Patients in group A (nonimmune retreatment) had progressed on first-line standard chemotherapy without prior exposure to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Patients in group B (Immunotherapy re-challenging) had progressed on first-line PD-1 antibody combined with chemotherapy, with optimal efficacy such as stable disease (SD), partial response (PR) or complete response (CR). Eligible patients had at least one measurable lesion (≥ 10 mm long diameter on CT scan for non-lymph node lesions and ≥ 15 mm short diameter on CT scan for lymph node lesions according to the iRECIST criteria). Other key inclusion criteria were an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG) of 0–1, adequate organ function, and a life expectancy of more than 3 months.

The key exclusion criteria included microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) or deficient mismatch repair (dMMR) status, active autoimmune disease or autoimmune disease with potential for recurrence, bleeding risk, coagulation disorders, thrombolytic therapy, a history of severe allergy, symptomatic brain or leptomeningeal metastases, any severe and/or uncontrolled disease such as poorly controlled blood pressure, uncontrolled infection, active hepatitis and a history of immunodeficiency.

All patients signed an informed consent form before enrollment in the trial. The Institutional Review Board and Ethics Committee of Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center approved the protocol (2208259-6). The trial was conducted in accordance with the International Conference on Harmonization (ICH) Guidelines for Good Clinical Practice (GCP) and the Declaration of Helsinki and Chinese law. This trial has been registered with CLINICALTRIALS. GOV (NCT06030934).

sec.title: Treatment procedure
sec.p: All patients received a combination of envafolimab (200 mg, sc, days 1 and 15, Q4W), lenvatinib (8 mg/12 mg, up to weight of pts, po, qd) and albumin-bound paclitaxel (100 mg/m2, IV, days 1, 8, and 15, Q4W, up to 6 cycles) for up to 2 years until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, patient death, or withdrawal of informed consent. Dose reduction was not permitted for envafolimab in this trial.

sec.title: Clinical outcomes
sec.p: Clinical oncologic imaging assessments were performed every 8 weeks during treatment according to the RECIST 1.1 and iRECIST criteria. Safety assessments were conducted via CTCAE 5.0, and adverse events were recorded throughout the trial up to 30 days after the end of treatment.

The primary endpoint was the ORR. The secondary endpoints included OS (the time from the date of informed consent to the date of death due to any cause), PFS (the time from the date of informed consent to any documented tumor progression or death due to any cause), DCR (including complete response, partial response cases and stable disease) and safety. Adverse effects (AEs) were classified and graded via the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (version 5.0).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Due to the exploratory nature of this trial, the target sample size was set at 30 patients (about 15 patients in each group), based on accrual time, the anticipated number of enrolled patients at the selected sites and limited funding. No formal power calculation was performed for the primary endpoint given the exploratory design.

Efficacy analysis was conducted in full analysis set (FAS), which included patients who met the eligibility criteria and received at least one cycle of chemotherapy with at least one post-baseline assessment. Safety analysis was performed on a safety set (SS), which included patients who received at least one cycle of chemotherapy.

Safety indicators included adverse events, laboratory tests, vital signs, electrocardiogram data, and etc. Efficacy analyses of PFS, OS, and ORR and safety analysis were performed. OS and PFS were estimated through the Kaplan–Meier method. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated via the stratified Cox proportional hazards model. The statistical significance level was set to 0.05. Statistical methods were analyzed by using Stata statistical software (version 12.0; Stata Corp, College Station, TX).

sec.title: Efficacy outcomes
sec.p:
At the data cutoff (September 14, 2024), 15 patients in Group A (100.0%) and 12 patients in Group B (80.0%) experienced disease progression or death. The median number of treatment cycles administered was 7. The ORR was 60.0% (9/15) in Group A and 46.7% (7/15) in Group B. The DCR was 100.0% (15/15) in Group A and 100.0% (15/15) in Group B (Table 2). In Group A, the mPFS was 8.2 months (95% CI 6.1–10.4 months; Fig. 2A), and the mOS was 14.8 months (95% CI 7.4–22.2 months; Fig. 2B). In Group B, the mPFS was 5.9 months (95% CI 3.8–8.1 months; Fig. 2C), and the mOS was 11.5 months (95% CI 3.1–19.9 months; Fig. 2D). While Group A showed numerically better outcomes than Group B (median PFS: 8.2 vs. 5.9 months; median OS: 14.8 vs. 11.5 months), there was no statistically significant difference in PFS (P = 0.629; Fig. 3A) or OS (P = 0.873; Fig. 3B) between the two groups. These findings should be interpreted with caution given the small sample size and potential baseline imbalances between groups.Table 2

In both groups, post-hoc subgroup analysis was performed to analyze the PFS and OS of the eligible patients according to Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) status, sex, age, primary tumor location, histologic grade, pathologic type, liver metastasis, lung metastasis, lymphatic metastasis, peritoneal metastasis and ascites. In Group A, there was no significant difference in survival according to the subgroup analysis. In Group B, patients with SRCC/mucinous adenocarcinoma had a significantly shorter PFS (P = 0.025) and OS (P = 0.038) than those with adenocarcinoma.

sec.title: Safety profile
sec.p:
All patients experienced treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs). The most common AEs (with an incidence of ≥ 5%) were summarized in Table 3. The incidence of grade 3/4 AEs was 93.3% (14/15) in Group A, and 86.7% (13/15) in Group B. In both groups, decreased white blood cell counts and decreased neutrophil counts were the most common grade 3/4 AEs. Five patients (33.3%) in Group A, and two patients (13.3%) in Group B experienced immune-related adverse events (irAEs), but none of them experienced irAEs of grade 3 or above (Supplementary Table 1).Table 3

sec.title: Albumin-bound paclitaxel can activate T cells and enhance the antitumor efficacy of PD-1 antibodies
sec.p:
In our preliminary work, we investigated the effects of chemotherapy drugs on T-cell activation and cytotoxic function. Initially, we activated T cells from commercially available fresh peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and transferred the activated T cells into culture media containing varying concentrations of chemotherapy drugs (albumin-bound paclitaxel, oxaliplatin, and fluorouracil) after 48 h to determine the maximum tolerated concentrations of these drugs for T cells. The experimental results revealed that the maximum tolerated concentrations for T cells were 10 nmol/L for both paclitaxel (Fig. 4A, B) and oxaliplatin (Fig. 4C), and 50 nmol/L for fluorouracil (Fig. 4D).Fig. 4
Counting T cells after culturing T cells in media containing varying concentrations of chemotherapy drugs for 48 h. The maximum tolerated concentrations for T cells were 10 nmol/L for paclitaxel (A), albumin-bound paclitaxel (B), oxaliplatin (C), and 50 nmol/L for fluorouracil (D)

In addition, both paclitaxel and albumin-bound paclitaxel could enhance the cytotoxic function of T cells at specific concentrations. T cells cultured at a concentration of 10 nmol/L of paclitaxel (Fig. 5A, B) and albumin-bound paclitaxel (Fig. 5C, D) exhibited significantly enhanced cytotoxicity against human gastric cancer cell lines (AGS and BGC-803). In contrast, T cells cultured with oxaliplatin (Fig. 5E, F) and fluorouracil (Fig. 5G, H) showed no significant difference in cytotoxicity against gastric cancer cells compared to regular T cells. Paclitaxel and albumin-bound paclitaxel not only increased T cell cytotoxicity, but also, when used in combination with a PD-1 antibody, augmented its anti-cancer effect on tumor cells that were sensitive to PD-1 antibody, whereas 5-FU and oxaliplatin did not (Fig. 6).Fig. 5
The effects of paclitaxel, albumin-bound paclitaxel, oxaliplatin, and fluorouracil on the cytotoxic function of T cells against gastric cancer cells. T cells cultured at a concentration of 10 nmol/L of paclitaxel (A/B) and albumin-bound paclitaxel (C/D) exhibited significantly enhanced cytotoxicity against AGS and BGC-803 cells. In contrast, T cells cultured with oxaliplatin (E/F) and fluorouracil (G/H) showed no significant difference in cytotoxicity against gastric cancer cells compared to control T cells (* P < 0.05, ** P < 0.01)Fig. 6
PD-1 antibody Plus Taxane Boosts T-Cell Killing. When PD-1 antibody was added to BGC-803 cells co-cultured with T cells that had been cultured with four different chemotherapeutic drugs respectively, the survival rate of gastric cancer cells was significantly decreased. The addition of paclitaxel or albumin-bound paclitaxel could further enhance the anticancer effect, while 5-Fu and oxaliplatin could not. (* P < 0.05, ** P < 0.01)

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In the second-line treatment setting, the effects of cytotoxic chemotherapy on OS are relatively modest, and treatments with paclitaxel, docetaxel, and irinotecan can result in a median OS ranging from 4.0 to 5.3 months. In the RAINBOW global phase III clinical trial, the median OS of patients treated with ramucirumab combined with paclitaxel versus those treated with placebo combined with paclitaxel was 9.6 months vs. 7.4 months (P = 0.017), achieving both primary endpoints of PFS and OS. The combination of paclitaxel and ramucirumab has become the standard second-line therapy [13]. The randomized phase III FRUTIGA study investigated the efficacy of fruquintinib in combination with paclitaxel versus paclitaxel alone in patients with advanced gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma who had exhibited disease progression after first-line standard chemotherapy. The FRUTIGA study demonstrated that combination treatment with fruquintinib and paclitaxel led to significant improvements in PFS, ORR, and DCR. The ORR for both groups was 42.5% vs. 22.4%, the DCR was 77.2% vs. 56.3%, and the median PFS was 5.6 months for the regimen combining fruquintinib and paclitaxel compared with 2.73 months for treatment with paclitaxel alone. However, there was no significant difference in median OS between the combination group and the paclitaxel monotherapy group (9.63 vs. 8.41 months; P = 0.6064) [15].

The efficacy of second-line treatments for GC remains limited. In light of this fact, we initiated this exploratory trial to assess the effects and safety of the combination of nab-paclitaxel with lenvatinib and envafolimab, with the aim of enhancing treatment outcomes.

In theory, there may be synergistic effects among antivascular therapy, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy. Both antivascular therapy and chemotherapy may enhance the efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 antibodies, and the combination of these three drugs may have better antitumor effects without overlapping toxicities [21].

Inhibiting angiogenesis is a key strategy in GC therapy, with such agents including anti-VEGF monoclonal antibodies, VEGF binding proteins, and VEGF receptor TKIs. Blockade of the VEGF pathway has the potential to reconfigure the immunosuppressive TME into one that is more conducive to immune responses or T-cell-mediated inflammation, thereby potentially increasing the efficacy of ICIs and expanding the patient population that may benefit from such treatments. Combining immunotherapeutic drugs with antiangiogenic agents can synergize their therapeutic benefits [22].

Representative antiangiogenic drugs, such as regorafenib, primarily suppress the activity of regulatory Tregs through VEGFR signaling and tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) via CSF1R signaling. This intervention modulates the immune microenvironment, thereby facilitating the activation and effectiveness of killer T cells targeted by PD-1 antibodies. The REGONIVO study targeted patients with AGC or colorectal cancer (CC). Fifty previously treated patients with advanced or metastatic GC or CC were enrolled to receive regorafenib combined with nivolumab treatment. The objective response rate (ORR) was 40%, and the disease control rate was 88%. The ORR of patients with GC was 44%, and the ORR of patients with CC was 36% [23]. Lenvatinib, a multikinase inhibitor that targets VEGF receptors and other receptor tyrosine kinases, has been shown to significantly reduce the number of tumor-associated macrophages and enhance the infiltration of CD8+ T cells, thereby augmenting the antitumor activity of PD-1 inhibitors. The combination of lenvatinib and pembrolizumab has demonstrated promising antitumor activity and an acceptable safety profile in patients with AGC, in both first-line and second-line treatment settings (EPOC1706) [24]. We selected lenvatinib rather than ramucirumab based on these immunomodulatory properties and the distinct mechanism of action as a multi-kinase inhibitor, though we acknowledge that direct comparative data between lenvatinib and ramucirumab in this setting are lacking.

Taxanes may also enhance the efficacy of immunotherapy. A recent study revealed the potential for developing novel T-cell–based therapeutic strategies in which T cells are treated ex vivo with optimal, stable doses of taxanes to maximize the induction of extracellular vesicle release. Published in Cancer Cell, this research demonstrated that taxanes can directly activate T cells to eliminate tumor cells by promoting the release of cytotoxic extracellular vesicles. This cytotoxic activity has potent therapeutic effects on organoid cultures derived from cancer patients and in mice bearing tumors. [25] Additionally, we conducted cellular experiments and found that nab-paclitaxel, at equivalent doses, has a T-cell-activating effect equivalent to that of conventional paclitaxel. Collectively, these findings suggest that the combination of paclitaxel with immunotherapy can further activate immune responses and potentially augment therapeutic outcomes. Nab-paclitaxel is not only less toxic but also enables patients to avoid the potential immunosuppressive effects associated with hormonal pretreatment. So, the therapeutic efficacy may be significantly enhanced by combining antiangiogenic therapy and immunotherapy with paclitaxel [26]. Our exploratory in vitro findings using commercially available PBMCs further support this mechanistic rationale and generate a testable hypothesis for the synergistic effect of albumin-bound paclitaxel and PD-L1 inhibition, which informed the design of our clinical combination regimen.

Our clinical trial is meticulously designed and grounded in the aforementioned theoretical frameworks. In Group A (ICI-naïve patients), we observed a median PFS of 8.2 months and ORR of 60.0%. These results appear favorable compared to historical controls (FRUTIGA: mPFS 5.6 months, ORR 42.5%; RAINBOW: mPFS 4.4 months, ORR 28%; REGARD: mPFS 2.1 months) [13–15]. The median OS of 14.8 months also exceeded historical reports. However, we emphasize that these cross-trial comparisons are limited by the single-center, non-randomized design, small sample size, and potential selection bias. The true efficacy of this regimen can only be determined through randomized controlled trials. Interestingly, even among patients who progressed on first-line PD-1 inhibitor therapy (Group B), the three-drug regimen yielded a median PFS of 5.9 months. While this was numerically inferior to Group A, the difference was not statistically significant (P = 0.629 for PFS; P = 0.873 for OS). The shorter median PFS in the ICI rechallenge group may be attributed to potential cross-resistance between PD-1 and PD-L1 inhibitors, or to baseline differences between groups (e.g., PD-L1 CPS availability, histologic subtypes). Caution is advised when drawing conclusions regarding PD-L1 rechallenge efficacy given these limitations and the small cohort size.

The overall incidence of adverse events (AEs) across all grades was 100%, with 80% of patients (n = 24) experiencing grade 3 or higher AEs during the treatment period. A total of seven patients (23.3%) in the two groups experienced immune-related adverse events below grade 3. Among them, there were five patients (33.3%) in Group A and two patients (13.3%) in Group B. This finding is similar to the research results of Checkmate 649. Most treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) of grade 3 or higher included neutropenia (56.25%) and leukopenia (37.5%). The most frequent ≥ grade 3 treatment-emergent adverse events were neutropenia (60.0%), leukopenia (42.9%) and anemia (11.7%) in the fruquintinib and paclitaxel groups of the FRUTIGA study [15]. Our triple-drug regimen did not augment the drug toxicity, and the tolerability profile was deemed acceptable.

This trial has several important limitations that must be acknowledged: (1) single-center, non-randomized design with inherent selection bias; (2) small sample size limiting statistical power and generalizability; (3) baseline imbalances between groups (e.g., PD-L1 CPS data availability, sex distribution); (4) open-label design; (5) exploratory nature without formal power calculation; and (6) limited follow-up duration, particularly for Group B. These limitations preclude definitive conclusions about comparative efficacy between groups or against standard of care.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Our finding revealed that triple-drug combination therapy demonstrated promising preliminary effects and safety in this second-line setting in patients of AGC, especially in those who have not previously received ICIs. However, these findings should be interpreted with caution given the single-center, non-randomized design and small sample size. Randomized controlled trials are warranted to confirm these results and identify predictive biomarkers.
